On the feast of the Synaxis of the Archangels the monastery holds its great festival, and sailors traditionally bring offerings in thanksgiving for protection at sea.
11-8.desc: Synaxis of the Archangel Michael at the monastery of Panormitis on the island of Symi.
11-8.name: Archangel Michael of Panormitis

11-8.bio:
The monastery of the Taxiarchs at Mantamados on Lesbos houses a celebrated relief icon of the Archangel Michael. Tradition relates that after a pirate raid on the monastery, a surviving monk shaped the icon from clay mixed with the blood of the slain brothers.

The icon is venerated as wonderworking, and the monastery keeps a great festival on the feast of the Archangels.
11-8.desc: Synaxis of the Archangel Michael the Taxiarch at Mantamados on Lesbos.
11-8.name: Archangel Michael of Mantamados

11-9.bio:
The holy apostle Onesiphoros, one of the Seventy, is remembered with honor by the Apostle Paul in his second epistle to Timothy. When Paul was imprisoned in Rome, Onesiphoros sought him out diligently and refreshed him, unashamed of the Apostle's chains, and Paul prayed that the Lord grant mercy to his whole household.

Tradition holds that he continued in apostolic labors and ended his life as a martyr for Christ. He is commemorated on November 9.
11-9.name: Onesiphoros the Apostle

11-9.bio:
St. Nektarios of Aegina, Metropolitan of Pentapolis, is one of the most beloved saints of modern Greece. Born in Selybria of Thrace in 1846, he served the Church with great humility and was slandered and unjustly removed from his see in Egypt, bearing the injustice without bitterness. He later taught in Athens and founded the Holy Trinity Convent on the island of Aegina, where he reposed in 1920.

Countless healings have been attributed to his intercession, and he is invoked especially by those suffering from cancer and serious illness. He was glorified as a saint by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1961, and his feast is a major name day for those named Nektarios and Nektaria.
11-9.desc: St. Nektarios of Aegina, Metropolitan of Pentapolis, wonderworker.
11-9.name: Nektarios of Aegina

11-9.bio:
Venerable Matrona was born at Perge in Pamphylia in the fifth century and was married in Constantinople. Longing for the monastic life, she left her husband and, disguised as a eunuch named Babylas, entered a men's monastery, where her identity was eventually discovered.

After years of wandering and ascetic struggle she founded a convent in Constantinople and guided many women in the spiritual life, reposing at a great age.
11-9.desc: Venerable Matrona of Perge, who lived disguised as a monk and later founded a convent in Constantinople.
11-9.name: Matrona of Constantinople

11-9.bio:
Saint Theoktiste was a young nun of Lesbos who was carried off by Arab raiders in the ninth century. Landed on the deserted island of Paros, she escaped and hid in the ruined church of the Panagia Ekatontapyliani, where she lived alone for some thirty-five years on wild plants and prayer.

Tradition relates that a hunter found her shortly before her death and, at her request, brought her Holy Communion, after which she reposed in peace.
11-9.desc: Venerable Theoktiste of Lesbos, who lived alone for thirty-five years on the island of Paros.
11-9.name: Theoktiste of Lesbos

11-9.bio:
Saint Eustolia was a Roman noblewoman who came to Constantinople to lead a life of asceticism. Sopatra, daughter of the Emperor Maurice, became her disciple, and together they founded a convent in the city.

Both reposed in peace in the seventh century after a life of prayer and charity.
11-9.desc: Venerable Eustolia and Sopatra, nuns of Constantinople.
11-9.name: Eustolia and Sopatra

11-9.bio:
Saint Symeon Metaphrastes was a high official at the Byzantine court in the tenth century and a man of great learning. He is remembered above all for compiling and rewriting the lives of the saints in the great collection known as the Menologion.

He also composed hymns and prayers still used in the Church, and reposed in peace.
11-9.desc: Venerable Symeon Metaphrastes, compiler of the lives of the saints.
11-9.name: Symeon Metaphrastes

11-9.bio:
Saint John Kolovos, called the Short or the Dwarf, was one of the great Desert Fathers of Scetis in Egypt in the fourth and fifth centuries. He was a disciple of Abba Ammoes and later the spiritual father of many monks.

The best-known story of his obedience relates that he watered a dry stick daily at his elder's command until it bore fruit. Many of his sayings are preserved in the Apophthegmata.
11-9.desc: Venerable John the Short of Scetis, disciple of Abba Ammoes and teacher of obedience.
11-9.name: John Kolovos

11-9.bio:
Venerable Euthymios was a companion of Saint Athanasios of Athos and served as steward, or docheiaris, of the Great Lavra before founding his own monastery, which took its name from his office. His nephew Neophytos succeeded him and completed the foundation on its present site.

Both are honoured on Mount Athos as the founders of Docheiariou.
11-9.desc: Venerable Euthymios and Neophytos, founders of the Docheiariou monastery on Mount Athos.
11-9.name: Euthymios and Neophytos of Docheiariou
